4 ♠ GTO CRASH COURSE - STRATEGY GUIDE


    VIDEO 1


  Game Theory Basics
  It's the buzzword heard
  around poker tables,         Coach:
  forums and training          Doug Hull
  sites: “GTO”. But what
                               Video Length:
  is it? You may know
                               23:53
  the acronym stands for
  “Game Theory Optimal”
  and can thus deduce that it refers to an optimal strategy
  derived from “game theory”, so what exactly is game
  theory?

  We felt any complete course on GTO play in poker should
  include a brief overview of what game theory actually is,
  hence this short introductory video from self-professed
  math geek Doug Hull. As Doug explains in his preamble,
  you won't learn much directly about poker from this video,
  but it does mean that the next time people are throwing
  around the term “GTO”, you'll probably be the only person
  in the conversation who knows what game theory is. From
  a more practical point of view, this video will give you
  some understanding of the scope and limitations of game
  theory as applied to the beautiful game of poker.

  If you're interested in the history and development of this
  field, the Wikipedia entry is excellent. For a dramatised
  version of one of the key mathematicians working in this
  area, the movie “A Beautiful Mind” may entertain.

## PDF page 5

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/GTO%20Crash%20Course%20Strategy%20Guide%20-%20Red%20Chip%20Poker.pdf#page=5)

```text
5 ♠ GTO CRASH COURSE - STRATEGY GUIDE



  Video Summary
  Game theory is the study of rational decision making.
  More explicitly, game theory is the mathematical modeling
  of the outcome of decisions, which provides a means for
  choosing which decision is optimal.

  Pay-off matrix: What is the result of each decision?
  In simple games (or more general processes involving
  decisions), we can summarize the possible outcomes
  using a pay-off matrix. It's simply a shorthand way of
  expressing outcomes that is convenient to manipulate
  mathematically.

  Poker is a game involving actions and responses. For
  example, we can choose to check or bet. If we check our
  opponent can check or bet. If we bet, our opponent can
  fold, call or raise. In games of this form, there will always
  be an optimal strategy. We check X% of the time and bet
  Y% of the time. When we check, our opponent similarly
  will check or bet in some ratio. When those percentages
  are optimized such that neither player can improve their
  outcome, we are at a Nash equilibrium.

  One of the most important concepts stemming from such
  a perfect strategy is the idea of indifference. When we
  employ the strategy at a Nash equilibrium, we do not care
  what our opponent does, because all decisions produce
  the same overall outcome. However, if our opponent is
  deviating from an optimal strategy, and we know in what
  manner they are deviating, we can develop a counter-
  strategy that exploits them more effectively than a GTO
  strategy.
```

## PDF page 6

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/GTO%20Crash%20Course%20Strategy%20Guide%20-%20Red%20Chip%20Poker.pdf#page=6)

```text
6 ♠ GTO CRASH COURSE - STRATEGY GUIDE


  If you've had some exposure to these ideas in the context
  of poker, this should sound somewhat familiar to you. If
  we do not know our opponent's strategy, or we suspect
  they are playing optimally, we are compelled to take a GTO
  approach. (A notable exception is when player pool data is
  sufficiently compelling that we can deviate even against
  an unknown player.) However, if we determine that our
  opponent is deviaiting from a GTO solution, we maximize
  our pay-off by following an exploitative strategy. And
  what is fascinating and critical is that typically this will
  not be a small deviation from the GTO solution, it'll be a
  thumping great big one.

  Here's a simple example. One of the applications of
  GTO to poker is that we can calculate optimal bluffing
  frequencies on, say, the river. Since these are GTO
  solutions, they assume that we are playing against a
  perfect (GTO) opponent. If we've arrived at the river
  with air, such analyses tell us how often we should bluff
  and how often we should give up. But what if we know
  something about our opponents' strategy?

  Suppose we know that if they check-call the flop and
  turn, they will either lead the river when they have a
  strong hand, or check and fold to a bet? Against such
  an opponent it is hopefully intuitively apparent that
  whenever they take a check-call/check-call/check line
  and we have 9-high, we should bluff 100% of the time.
  And notice we are not doing so because it is our “only
  chance to the win the hand”. We're taking this action
  because our opponent has deviated from GTO and we
  maximize our long-term expectation by always bluffing.
```

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/GTO%20Crash%20Course%20Strategy%20Guide%20-%20Red%20Chip%20Poker.pdf#page=7)

```text
7 ♠ GTO CRASH COURSE - STRATEGY GUIDE


  This particular case may seem trivial and self-evident. If
  villain always folds, we should bluff all our air. But here's
  where things get really fascinating for poker players
  interested in making money. It turns out we don't need
  our opponent to always fold in this spot. In fact, if they
  fold even slightly more than Nash equlibrium dictates, we
  should still bluff 100% of the time.

  So what can we conclude from this? One argument you
  may have heard is that, since none of our opponents are
  perfect, they do not play GTO, thus we shouldn't either.
  That's fine as far as it goes, but notice that in order to find
  the correct exploit against a non-perfect opponent, the
  one critical piece of information we need is what the GTO
  strategy is. Without this information we cannot deviate
  and develop the maximal exploit.



  Push-fold as a poker example
  While GTO solvers are now the favorite toys of cash-
  game theorists, game theory has been applied to poker
  for decades. David Sklansky pioneered this work in the
  context of limit poker where the fixed bet size makes
  analytical solutions possible. In No Limit, iterative
  algoritms are required to zero in on the Nash solutions.
  Such studies were first carried out in short-stacked
  tournament situations. Because such situations are
  essentially one street poker (all the action is preflop), they
  require less computational power and could be attacked
  by desktop computers fifteen years ago. It's only relatively
  recently that tools like GTO+ allow people like you and me
  to carry out multi-street analyses in our dressing gowns.
```

## PDF page 8

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/GTO%20Crash%20Course%20Strategy%20Guide%20-%20Red%20Chip%20Poker.pdf#page=8)

```text
8 ♠ GTO CRASH COURSE - STRATEGY GUIDE


  The simplified model of blind versus blind play in the
  video illustrates the fundamental principles at work in
  short-stacked GTO solutions. However, in multi-street
  situations a critical feature is that there is dead money in
  the pot from previous streets. It's the amount of this dead
  money relative to our bets (and in some cases remaining
  stacks) that impacts GTO solutions such as our bluffing
  frequency.

  As we'll see later in this course, these studies have
  revealed that when we view poker as a range vs range
  battle, we require mixed strategies. That is the GTO
  solution includes, for example, sometimes checking
  and sometimes betting in a given situation. Much of
  the challenge of incorporating GTO ideas in poker is
  decoding the output of solvers into a form that a human
  can practically apply. We'll explore these ideas in the
  remainder of the course.
```
